sheet-39-3.description: The lower part of sheet 39 is a separate area south west of the Green at 100 feet to an inch, with north up, divided from the main part by a heavy line. South Street runs from the top to the bottom edge at the middle of the part, with Vine Street at the top, Walnut Street crossing it near the centre and Woodland Avenue leaving it to the south east. At the left, Whitney Avenue and Prospect Place run down the sheet, and Bellevue Park, a platted tract of long narrow lots in blocks 21, 22 and 24, lies between them and South Street. Walnut Street is marked not graded, as are parts of Whitney Avenue and Prospect Place. The Bellevue Park lots are mostly vacant, apart from John Macintyre's greenhouses beside South Street, and the South Street Township School at the bottom. East of South Street the Madison Avenue Dairy of J. F. Burt stands with its watchman, lighting and steam notes. Woodland Avenue runs south east to the works of A. V. R. Wulff, cleaning works, on a row of long lots in block 16 beside Degan's Lane, a lane with house numbers from 501 to 518. A north arrow stands in the block marked 15.
notes: Walnut is today Sand Hill Road; Degan's Lane is Degan Lane.
The modern node of Degan Lane and Woodland Avenue is about 15 m from the drawn junction and was not used.

sheet-40-3.description: This part, in the lower left of sheet 40, shows the works of the Butters Aluminum Bronze Works at Jefferson Crossing in Hanover Township, about three miles east of Morristown, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Jefferson Crossing Road runs down the right side of the part and the Morristown and Erie Railroad crosses it diagonally in the lower right, with a switch track curving off into the works. The works consist of rows of small one-storey buildings: grinding rooms, bolters, curing rooms and polishing rooms along a driveway, a melting house, a warehouse, an office and a wash house, together with several outlined proposed buildings and a proposed extension. A driven well is marked in the yard. A note gives the fire protection: a night watchman, steam heat, chemical extinguishers and corrugated galvanized iron construction on studding. The rest of the part is blank.

sheet-41-1.description: Sheet 41 shows Normandy Heights, an area of large country estates east of Morristown, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north to the left. Columbia Road runs diagonally up the left half of the sheet and Normandy Heights Road curves down through the middle from their junction with Normandy Parkway near the top. The estates are named with their owners: Featherleigh Farm of J. A. H. Hopkins with its hennery and tool house; Thorn Oaks of W. V. S. Thorn; the house of Peter H. B. Frelinghuysen; Edgewood of O. C. Billings; Ellerslea of C. W. Armour; the house of Jos. B. Dickson; Greystone of Jesse L. Eddy; Wyndmoor of J. B. Dickson; and Lannock of A. C. Humphreys. Garages, stables, gasoline tanks and a swimming pool are drawn beside several of the houses, and water pipes from a stand pipe cross the open ground. A boxed inset at the right, a separate part, shows Cedar Court of O. H. Kahn.

The road printed Normandy P'kway north-east of the junction matches the modern Normandy Heights Road, and the road printed Normandy Heights R'd matches the modern Normandy Parkway.

sheet-42-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 42 is the eastern half of the Whippany sheet, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned so that north points up and to the right. It lies to the right of a vertical heavy line and below the Malapardis inset, and is bounded on its upper left by the Muir mill octagon. Newark & Mount Pleasant Pike runs diagonally down the part from the upper left to Troy Road at the lower right, with a water main along it. The Whippany River winds down the middle of the part, west of the Pike. The largest works shown is the Hanover Mills of the United Paper Board Co., a long brick paper machine building with a machine shop, supply house, engine room, finishing room, store house and a long storage shed, served by a side track of the Morristown and Erie railroad, with hydrants, a head race and a tail race. North of it the Whippany Presbyterian Church stands near the Pike; at the southern end the Whippany Methodist Church, its parsonage and a few dwellings face Troy Road. Scattered dwellings and outbuildings line both sides of the Pike, numbered along it. A compass rose and the lines of a roadway to the school house fill the open ground. Block numbers 78 and 79 are printed in the large unbuilt areas. The line work is lighter than on the 50 ft sheets of the town. Control is the junction of the Pike with the school roadway and with Troy Road.
notes: The Newark & Mt. Pleasant Pike here corresponds to the modern NJ 10 (Whippany Road and Mount Pleasant Avenue); Troy R'd matches the modern Troy Hills Road.

sheet-42-5.description: Part 5 of sheet 42 is the western half of the Whippany sheet, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north nearly at the top. It occupies the left side of the sheet below the Hanover High School inset and wraps around the left and lower edges of the Muir mill octagon. Rasippany Road runs down the part from top to bottom, crossing Newark & Mount Pleasant Pike near the upper left and the Whippany River and the Morristown and Erie railroad about midway, and ending at Morristown Road along the bottom edge. Whippany is mainly an industrial village. The works at the lower left are the Caledonian Mills of the United Paper Board Co., a paper machine room with loading shed, storage and head and tail races at the river. Near the Pike is the feed, coal and wood yard of Geo. F. Freeman, a barber, and a pool room. Dwellings, many numbered along the roads, are scattered through the open lots. St. Mary's R.C. Church is at the lower left. The part carries the title and descriptive text for Whippany: population 800, a volunteer fire department being organised, water pressure and street conditions. Blocks 64 to 67 are printed in the open ground. Control is a single junction, that of the Pike with Rasippany Road.

sheet-43-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 43 shows the centre of Morris Plains at the Five Points, where Hanover Avenue, Speedwell Avenue and Dover Road meet. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned so that north is up and slightly to the left. Hanover Avenue runs across the part from side to side with its numbered lots, with a water main along it. Speedwell Avenue crosses it from top to bottom and runs south to Gregory Avenue, where a second heavy dividing line bounds the part. Dover Road leaves the Five Points to the upper left at an angle. The most important buildings are St. Virgil's Roman Catholic Church with its parochial school, convent and rectory on the west side of Speedwell Avenue, and the house called The Cross Ways of W. D. Ward on the north side. A fire alarm station with a suspended locomotive tire stands at the Five Points. East of Speedwell Avenue there is a nursery in block 108, a private entrance and a row of dwellings along Hanover Avenue and Gregory Avenue, with a few stores near the right edge. Block numbers 107 to 116 are printed. The top of the sheet carries a small key map of the town, which is a separate part. Control is one junction only, at the Five Points.

sheet-43-3.description: Part 3 of sheet 43 covers the western side of Morris Plains along Hanover Avenue, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 15 degrees. It lies below the heavy stepped dividing line that crosses the sheet and takes in the lower third. Hanover Avenue runs across the bottom with a water main. Maple Avenue runs parallel to it above the block between Stiles Avenue on the left and Concord Place on the right, a small subdivision of narrow lots (block 103) with dwellings along its lower edge. Stiles Avenue and Concord Place run down from Maple Avenue to Hanover Avenue; Lake Road and Sherman Roadway continue south from Hanover Avenue at the bottom edge. At the lower left the Morristown Township Public School, a brick building heated by steam, stands on Hanover Avenue, and nearby are dwellings of blocks 109 and 110. Along the lower right edge are a mason's shop for cement work and dwellings of block 111. The large blocks 101, 102 and 116 are mostly open, with a cemetery and dwellings scattered on them. A scale bar, the copyright note and the Map Division stamp are printed in the margin. The Five Points part of the same sheet lies above. Control is four junctions of Hanover Avenue and Maple Avenue with Stiles Avenue and Concord Place.

sheet-44-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 44 shows the industrial strip of Morris Plains along the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad east of the village centre, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Hanover Avenue crosses the top of the part with a water main, and the railroad, a fan of tracks, crosses it on a concrete bridge at the upper left. On the south side of the avenue stands the Arrowsmith Mfg. Co. Inc., makers of arch supports and foot specialties, a group of finishing, packing, printing, stock, blanking and gas producer buildings with a coal shed. Farther right along the railroad the Morris Plains Lumber & Coal Co. has lumber sheds, a shingle shed and large coal sheds on piers, with an average stock of 400,000 feet of lumber, served by side tracks. A blind water course and a sewer pipe run from top to bottom through the right half. Gregory Avenue is drawn only by dashed lines at the left. A compass rose and a scale of feet occupy the open ground, and the Shonghum inset lies above at the right. Lots on Hanover Avenue are numbered 1206 to 1218. sheet-44-5.description: Part 5 of sheet 44 is the bottom strip of the sheet, titled Wilsonville, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 25 degrees. It shows the open fields of the New Jersey State Hospital for the Insane, with a village-like row of streets on the edge of the hospital grounds. Hanover Avenue runs across the part, curving at the right where an entrance to the hospital grounds leaves it. Willson Avenue runs below it, and 3rd Street, 2nd Street and 1st Street cross between them, enclosing blocks 121, 122 and 123 of dwellings, barns and sheds, some with lots laid out in the rear. Corner markers lettered A to E and circled numbers 28 to 30 and 1 to 4 are printed at the street corners. Along Hanover Avenue east of 1st Street a row of dwellings, an ice cream and tobacco shop and other small buildings is numbered 213 to 225, and a fire alarm station is at 2nd Street. Block 120 lies to the left and 123 to the right. The text gives the location as one and a quarter miles west of the Morris Plains station and states that the fire protection of the State Hospital is available. Control is two junctions on Hanover Avenue, with 1st Street and with 2nd Street.
notes: Hanover Avenue here is the modern West Hanover Avenue; 1st Street and 2nd Street keep their names.

sheet-45-1.description: Sheet 45 shows the northern end of Morris Plains along Speedwell Avenue, drawn at 50 feet to an inch (the sheet label says 100 ft only for the inset at the upper right) and turned about 15 degrees. Speedwell Avenue runs down the right side beside the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, whose tracks, side track and a concrete platform with a freight house lie on the right edge. Mayfair Road curves across the upper part into a private driveway, and the block of large houses between Mayfair Road and Jaqui Avenue, numbered block 94, holds several dwellings. Jaqui Avenue crosses the middle of the sheet. South of it block 96 holds, along the east side of Speedwell Avenue, a row of stores in brick, including a meat market, plumber, shoe store, grocery, bake shop, grain warehouse, post office and barber, with a garage of D. M. Merchant and the residence of D. M. Merchant. Franklin Place runs along the lower edge and Keenan Place meets it at the lower left. At the right, Littleton Road curves around a park and drives to the station. A small boxed inset at the upper right shows Rosedale Avenue and the Morris Plains Presbyterian Church. Control is the junctions of Speedwell Avenue with Mayfair Road, Jaqui Avenue and Franklin Place, and Franklin Place with Keenan Place.

sheet-46.description: Sheet 46 continues Morris Plains south along Speedwell Avenue, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 15 degrees. Speedwell Avenue runs down the middle of the sheet. On its east side lies block 99, bounded by the railroad of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western, with the D.L.&W.R.R. Station and its platform at the top, a triangle laid out as a park with drives to the station, Laurie's Garage in hollow tile, an office and a few stuccoed dwellings. Morris Plains Avenue and Academy Place cross at the bottom right, with the Morris Plains Academy, which is heated by steam, in block 105. West of Speedwell Avenue the sheet shows Franklin Place at the top with its row of dwellings, among them a Fire Dept. station house with a fire alarm station, a proposed street, block 98, and Glenbrook Place (Central Av.) with block 104 below it and a private driveway. Houses are mostly detached dwellings in frame and stucco. Block numbers 98, 99, 104 and 105 are printed and the sheet number 45 is shown at the top edge for the sheet above. Control is four points along Speedwell Avenue, two of them detected and two hand-picked, so rotation and scale are set only loosely.
notes: Glenbrook Place (Central Av.) is the modern Glenbrook Road; Academy Place is the modern Academy Road.

sheet-47.description: Sheet 47 shows Mount Tabor, the Methodist camp meeting village in Parsippany-Troy Hills, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 37 degrees. The compass rose at the left points to the upper left. Morristown Pike runs down the left edge and Newton Avenue parallel to it, a curving road that is the village's western boundary. Strowbridge Avenue runs down the centre and is crossed by Banghart Place, Morris Avenue, West Hedding Place, Summerfield Avenue, St. John's Avenue and Ridgewood Avenue, enclosing blocks 373 to 379 of small frame cottages. The curving Embury Place and Asbury Place run to the upper right toward Station Road, which leads to the Mt. Tabor Station. At the upper right are W. F. Headley's garage and a block of the camp meeting grounds with a bakery, general store and shop of Elmer Dickerson. A text block gives the water, fire and street details: two wells and two springs, a stand pipe of 140,000 gallons, the volunteer fire department of forty members, and the streets earth graded except Morris Pike, which is paved. Athletic fields lie at the bottom right and a public school at the left. The heavy line at the right divides the sheet from sheet 48. Control is eight junctions on Strowbridge Avenue and Newton Avenue.
notes: Newton Av. matches the modern Simpson Avenue and Morristown Pike the modern Tabor Road; Summerfield Av. is the modern Somerfield Avenue.

sheet-48.description: Sheet 48 shows the central part of Mount Tabor, the Methodist camp meeting village, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 38 degrees. The heart of the sheet is Trinity Park, a rounded open ground with the post office and auditorium, a tabernacle and a library, lying between Wesley Place and Fletcher Place. Simpson Avenue runs across the upper left, with the entrance to the camp ground and the Arlington hotel at the left edge. Fletcher Place, Whitefield Place and Boehm Avenue run down to Morris Avenue between blocks of small cottages (blocks 358 to 361), Dickerson Avenue crosses the top right with Force Place, Clark Place and Shaw Place behind it, and Butler Pass runs down the right side. Below Morris Avenue, East Hedding Place and West Hedding Place, North Place and Summerfield Avenue cross the blocks 367 to 371, and Reservoir Park holds the reservoir, a stand pipe and a valve pit. St. John's Avenue closes the sheet at the bottom, with blocks 349 to 351 and St. Peters Road at the right edge. Most buildings are frame cottages, with a few stores. Control is eleven junctions, mainly around Reservoir Park and Simpson Avenue; Mc Clintock Place, Shaw Place and Butler Pass were left out of the control.
